description: We are an interdisciplinary team of engineers and developers from IGDTUW specializing in AI/ML, full-stack systems, and geospatial data analytics. For NASA Space Apps 2026, we are building EMBERWISE—a clock-aware satellite data harmonization engine that unifies 20+ years of MODIS and VIIRS satellite active fire records to empower global climate scientists and emergency responders
summary:
EMBERWISE is a web app that joins 26 years of MODIS and VIIRS satellite fire detections for Punjab and Haryana into one continuous record. MODIS (1 km pixels, from 2000) and VIIRS (375 m pixels, from 2012) cannot simply be added: splicing them creates a false jump around 2012, which we call the Phantom Surge. We count burning H3 tiles per local solar day, learn a MODIS-to-VIIRS conversion on 2012 to 2019 (before Terra and Aqua drifted), and show every estimate with a range and a trust score.

Our Fire Clock Dial shows when each satellite looked, making Terra’s earlier and Aqua’s later overpass times visible. It is a diagnostic, not a correction. When Suomi NPP stopped delivering on 2 Nov 2026, we tested a handover to NOAA-20: rebuilding a season from NOAA-20 alone changed season totals by about 2 to 3%.

This matters because fire trends, smoke and air-quality studies depend on records that stay comparable as satellites age and retire. EMBERWISE is a research tool, not an official fire alert.

It’s well inside the 1,500-character limit. If the form counts differently or you want it shorter, tell me and I’ll trim it.
details:
What it does and how it works

EMBERWISE turns raw NASA FIRMS hotspot files into one continuous fire record for Punjab and Haryana, from Nov 2000 to Nov 2026. Each hotspot is cleaned, clipped to state boundaries and given a local solar time and date (UTC time plus longitude/15 hours). We then count burning tile-days: one H3 resolution-6 tile (about 36 km²) with at least one clean hotspot on one local day. Tiles remove the pixel-size difference between MODIS (1 km) and VIIRS (375 m). We never add MODIS and VIIRS counts, because they see the same fires. We learn a MODIS-to-VIIRS ratio per zone and calendar month on 2012 to 2019, before Terra and Aqua drifted, and apply it to earlier years. Every number is labelled Measured, Estimated, Indicative or Provisional and shown with a range and a trust score.

The app shows the naive splice next to the harmonized line (the Phantom Surge), a calendar, a hex map, a this-month-vs-usual card, a relay timeline with a Sensor-Loss toggle, a Fire Clock Dial, and a Transparency Lab that shows our own tests, including the ones we fail. Raw hotspot CSVs can be downloaded per area and year.

Handover after 2 Nov 2026

Suomi NPP’s last data is dated 2 Nov 2026. We chose NOAA-20 as the relay (13.15 h mean local time against a 13:30 target, 8 shared seasons with Suomi NPP), marked Provisional. Rebuilding a season from NOAA-20 alone changed season totals by about 2 to 3%; day-by-day agreement was 0.986 for 2025 and 0.81 for a held-out 2021.

Benefits and intended impact

Researchers, air-quality analysts and agencies need fire records that stay comparable as satellites age and retire. EMBERWISE shows where the record is solid and where it is not, and gives anyone the raw data to check it. It is a research and historical tool, not an official fire alert, perimeter map or emergency tool.

What is creative

The Fire Clock treats observation time as data. We measured that Terra’s median local hour fell from about 10.9 to about 9.25 and Aqua’s rose from about 13.3 to about 15.3 by 2026, so MODIS after about 2022 cannot be compared with earlier MODIS. The dial shows this openly, and because we learn the conversion before the drift, it does not enter the headline index. We also report failures: the conversion overshoots on peak days in Indian Punjab (about 61% error per day), so the index is capped and peak days before 2012 are upper-end estimates.

Tools

Python with polars and H3 for the pipeline; static JSON files with no backend; Vite, React, TypeScript and Tailwind, d3 scales and hand-written SVG, a Canvas hex map, and an installable offline PWA; GitHub for the repository. The data are NASA FIRMS (MODIS Collection 6.1, VIIRS Collection 2), with Survey of India state boundaries. AI assistants (Claude) were used for code help, checking analysis and drafting documentation; team members ran the code and own the results.

Factors we considered

  • Burning has shifted later in the day, so a learned ratio may partly reflect habit and not just sensor difference. We plot the ratio by year and state this limit.
  • At the seasonal peak many tiles burn, so tile-days flatten. We show the fraction of tiles burning beside the index.
  • Near-real-time files have no type field and do not overlap with standard data, so we apply a static-source mask to all eras and mark the near-real-time seam as untested.
  • Days with no rows are shown as gaps, not zeros.
  • Phones and weak connections: small pre-aggregated files, offline use, and hotspot CSVs loaded only on click.
